rv.q: Despite a stumble on the late preview to which critics were invited, it’s an astonishing, deeply moving piece of theatre.
But the evening’s power is undeniable.
But this is a seriously good play, seriously well acted, seriously well staged.
Seen here, Miller’s coruscating takedown of the American dream feels like a play for our time.
With a world-class cast led by Bryan Cranston and directed by the formidable Ivo van Hove, this is a must-see performance of the season.
These are two immensely powerful and gripping hours; I have quite simply never seen a better production of this play.
There’s an almost unbearable heaviness to Ivo van Hove’s powerful revival of All My Sons, staged with a crushing gravity underneath a giant glowing sun.
Here is acting and a production that takes Miller away from finger-wagging into essential truth-telling.

As we watch them all rip themselves and each other apart on a stage littered with red autumn leaves that irresistibly recall memorial poppy fields, this brutal dismantling of the American dream feels more pertinent than ever.
It has demanded that attention must be paid from the very start.
Respectful to the original story while bringing it into the 21st Century, All My Sons is a triumph.
Each element of the mise-en-scène works perfectly in tune with the other, delivering a simply arresting theatrical event.
And here Van Hove has brought together a cast and crew that demonstrate just why the play endures, delivering an exceptional production.

Director trusts material as written implicitly, no doubt knowing that his extraordinary cast will deliver with minimal artifice in one of the purest and most overpowering productions I have seen all year.
Yet in Miller’s diabolically brilliant text, he also emits such a man’s ability to project guilt on another: pure politician.
Arthur Miller's play All My Sons gives us strong reasons why we need to change the system we live under. Everyone should see it.
The production balances the inherent drama of tragedy with the intensity of quiet humanity without being melodramatic, demanding the audience’s attention and investment from the start.

Written in 1947, Arthur Miller's breakout play depicts a nation given over to deception and rapacity that responds only to one God - money - and this play, and van Hove's merciless take on it, should be required viewing now more than ever.

There’s nothing bigger than family, Chris tells his father, but in trying to secure their future, this family cannot escape the past, and in striving so hard to free themselves from it, van Hove’s absorbing revival only brings a terrible reckoning.
Van Hove’s cranky decisions can’t mar the power of the play’s thrilling finale.
